job.style: a comparison of two related ideas

passage: Matter is composed of tiny, discrete particles that are always in motion, rather than being a continuous solid block. When we heat a substance, these individual particles gain kinetic energy and move faster, but the particles themselves do not grow in size. During a phase change, such as ice melting into water, the temperature remains constant because the heat energy is used to overcome the forces of attraction between particles instead of increasing their motion. This explains why a substance does not get hotter while changing state. Furthermore, evaporation is a surface phenomenon that occurs at any temperature below the boiling point. It happens because particles at the surface gain enough energy to escape into the air. This process is influenced by humidity; when the air is already saturated with water vapor, it becomes harder for liquid particles to escape, thus slowing down evaporation. Finally, gases are highly compressible not because the particles are soft, but because there is significant empty space between them. When pressure is applied, these particles are simply pushed closer together, reducing the volume they occupy. Understanding that particles are distinct units with space between them is essential to grasping how matter behaves under different conditions of heat and pressure.

items.evidence: During a phase change, such as ice melting into water, the temperature remains constant because the heat energy is used to overcome the forces of attraction between particles instead of increasing their motion.
items.q: Why does the temperature of melting ice stay the same while heat is supplied?
options: Heat is spent loosening particles from each other
Heat is spent making each particle grow bigger
Heat is lost to the air around the ice
Heat only raises temperature in the solid state
items.explain: During melting, heat energy overcomes the forces between particles instead of making them move faster.

wrong.why: thinks heat escapes, so nothing changes
thinks heat always raises temperature, but only in some states

items.evidence: When pressure is applied, these particles are simply pushed closer together, reducing the volume they occupy.
items.q: A syringe full of air is pressed with the nozzle closed. What happens inside?
options: Air particles are pushed closer together
Air particles are squeezed into smaller sizes
Air particles are pushed out through the walls
Air particles stop moving and stick together
items.explain: Pressure pushes gas particles closer together, which reduces the volume they occupy.

wrong.why: thinks gas particles are soft and squishy
thinks particles leave a closed container
thinks particles stop moving when pressed

items.evidence: This process is influenced by humidity; when the air is already saturated with water vapor, it becomes harder for liquid particles to escape, thus slowing down evaporation.
items.q: Wet clothes are hung out on a very humid day. How will they dry?
options: More slowly than on a dry day
Faster than on a dry day
Only once the water starts boiling
At the same speed as on a dry day
items.explain: Humid air is already full of water vapor, so liquid particles escape harder and drying slows down.

wrong.why: thinks evaporation needs the boiling point
thinks air moisture makes no difference

items.evidence: Matter is composed of tiny, discrete particles that are always in motion, rather than being a continuous solid block.
items.q: A sugar cube dissolves in water without stirring. Which idea explains this best?
options: Its tiny particles keep moving and spread out
Its particles are held still until water arrives
Its particles are filled in with water
Its single block slowly turns into liquid
items.explain: Matter is made of tiny particles always in motion, so sugar particles can spread through the water.

wrong.why: thinks particles in a solid never move
thinks gaps between particles are filled
thinks matter is one continuous block

items.evidence: When we heat a substance, these individual particles gain kinetic energy and move faster, but the particles themselves do not grow in size.
items.q: A metal rod is heated. How do its particles change?
options: They move faster but stay the same size
They stay still but grow a little larger
They move faster and grow a little larger
They stay the same but move farther apart
items.explain: Heating gives particles more energy so they move faster, but the particles themselves do not grow.

wrong.why: thinks solid particles do not move
thinks particles move and also expand
thinks matter is a block with no particle motion
